- "[full content as above]"

This budget is intentionally tight: it is enough to execute every subtask once with occasional retries, but not enough to repeat any subtask repeatedly or restart the entire plan. You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

## Navigation policy

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

# Malko Competition Winners List (1965–2024)

## Overview
The **Malko Competition for Young Conductors** is a prestigious triennial international competition organized by the Danish National Symphony Orchestra (DR SymfoniOrkestret). It was founded in 1965 to honor the orchestra’s first principal conductor, **Nicolai Malko**. The competition identifies and promotes emerging conducting talent from around the world.

## Reliable Sources
1. **Official Malko Competition Website** – [All Winners page](https://malkocompetition.dk/winners/all) (lists first‑prize winners from 1965 to 2024, excluding 2001).
2. **Wikipedia** – [Malko Competition article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malko_Competition) (provides a detailed table with year, recipient, lifetime, nationality, and notes, including the 2001 edition where no first prize was awarded).

## Complete List of Laureates (First‑Prize Winners)

| Year | Laureate | Nationality | Notes |
|------|----------|-------------|-------|
| 1965 | Ralf Weikert | Austria | |
| 1968 | Avi Ostrowsky | Israel | |
| 1971 | Winston Dan Vogel | United States | |
| 1974 | Gotthard Lienicke | *Nationality not specified in sources* | |
| 1977 | Philip Barry Greenberg | United States | |
| 1980 | Maximiano Valdés | Chile | |
| 1983 | Claus Peter Flor | East Germany (now Germany) | |
| 1986 | Kazufumi Yamashita | Japan | |
| 1989 | Fabio Mechetti | Brazil | |
| 1992 | Jin Wang | Austria | |
| 1995 | Jan Wagner | Venezuela | |
| 1998 | Seikyo Kim | Japan | |
| 2001 | *No first prize awarded* | – | Second prize awarded to **Josep Caballé Domenech** (Spain). |
| 2005 | Mei‑Ann Chen | United States | |
| 2009 | Joshua Weilerstein | United States | |
| 2012 | Rafael Payare | Venezuela | |
| 2015 | Tung‑Chieh Chuang | Taiwan | |
| 2018 | Ryan Bancroft | United States | |
| 2021 | Dmitry Matvienko | Belarus | |
| 2024 | Samuel Seungwon Lee | South Korea | |

## Key Observations
- The competition is held **every three years**, with the most recent edition in 2024.
- The **2001 edition** did not award a first prize; the highest award (second prize) went to Spanish conductor Josep Caballé Domenech. This entry is included in the Wikipedia table but omitted on the official “All Winners” page.
- Nationalities are as listed in the sources; for **Gotthard Lienicke (1974)**, the nationality is not provided in either source.
- The list above represents **first‑prize (gold medal) winners**; many editions also awarded second, third, and audience prizes.

Both sources are highly reliable; the Wikipedia page is more complete for historical accuracy, while the official site is the authoritative presentation from the competition organizers.

function.name: mcp_get_article_history
function.description:
Get historical version of a Wikipedia page closest to the specified date.

        This tool provides historical Wikipedia article retrieval with:
        - Date-based version lookup
        - Auto-suggestion support
        - Multi-language support
        - LLM-optimized result formatting
        - Error handling

        If exact date version is not available, returns the closest version before that date.
        Supports auto-suggestion and redirects to handle company name changes or variations.

        Args:
            title: The title of the Wikipedia page
            date: Target date in YYYY/MM/DD format
            language: Language code for Wikipedia
            auto_suggest: Whether to use Wikipedia's auto-suggest and handle redirects
            output_format: Format for the response output

        Returns:
            ActionResponse with historical article content and metadata

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

message.content:
**Malko Competition Recipients (1965–2024)**

Compiled from the official Malko Competition website (https://malkocompetition.dk/winners/all) and the Wikipedia page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malko_Competition).  
Where both sources list the same year, the official website’s data is used for name and nationality, except that “Brasil” has been anglicised to “Brazil”.  
The 2001 winner is only listed on Wikipedia (no first prize was awarded that year; Caballé‑Domenech received the highest (2nd) prize).

| Year | Full Name | Nationality |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| 1965 | Ralf Weikert | Austria |
| 1968 | Avi Ostrowsky | Israel |
| 1971 | Winston Dan Vogel | United States |
| 1974 | Gotthard Lienicke | — |
| 1977 | Philip Greenberg | United States |
| 1980 | Maximiano Valdes | Chile |
| 1983 | Claus Peter Flor | Germany |
| 1986 | Kazufumi Yamashita | Japan |
| 1989 | Fabio Mechetti | Brazil |
| 1992 | Jin Wang | Austria |
| 1995 | Jan Wagner | Venezuela |
| 1998 | Seikyo Kim | Japan |
| 2001 | Josep Caballé Domenech | Spain |
| 2005 | Mei‑Ann Chen | United States |
| 2009 | Joshua Weilerstein | United States |
| 2012 | Rafael Payare | Venezuela |
| 2015 | Tung‑Chieh Chuang | Taiwan |
| 2018 | Ryan Bancroft | United States |
| 2021 | Dmitry Matvienko | Belarus |
| 2024 | Samuel Seungwon Lee | South Korea |

1. WebSurfer: Search the web to find a reliable list or information source detailing the recipients (winners/laureates) of the Malko Competition, including their names, the year they received the award, and their nationality as recorded at the time of the award.
2. WebSurfer: Extract and compile the specific data for all identified Malko Competition recipients from the source(s) found, focusing on capturing for each entry: the full name, the award year, and the nationality listed.
3. Reasoner [dep:2]: Analyze the compiled list of recipients. Filter the list to include only those recipients who received the award in the 20th Century and specifically after the year 1977 (i.e., award years from 1978 to 1999, inclusive).
4. Reasoner [dep:3]: From the filtered list of 20th-century (post-1977) recipients, identify which recipients have a nationality on record that corresponds to a country that no longer exists (e.g., Soviet Union, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, etc.).
5. Reasoner [dep:4]: Determine if, among the recipients identified in the previous step, there is exactly one unique individual. If multiple are found, identify the conflict. If only one is found, confirm this matches the user's query for "the only Malko Competition recipient" meeting the criteria.
6. Reasoner [dep:5]: For the single, confirmed recipient identified, extract and state their first name.

## Overview
The **Malko Competition for Young Conductors** is a prestigious triennial international competition organized by the Danish National Symphony Orchestra (DR SymfoniOrkestret). It was founded in 1965 to honor the orchestra’s first principal conductor, **Nicolai Malko**. The competition identifies and promotes emerging conducting talent from around the world.

1. **Official Malko Competition Website** – [All Winners page](https://malkocompetition.dk/winners/all) (lists first‑prize winners from 1965 to 2024, excluding 2001).
